utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise the general area on this particular map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm calling your attention to the two dots in that particular area. Did you notice any -- any particular activity going on there between July 12th and November 1st, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I did not notice any activity in the area nor did anybody inform me of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to learn that those are mass graves, it's the submission of the Prosecution, that were dug between 13 July and 17 July 1995, and contained thousands of bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: It would not surprise me because I was -- I learnt about that fact at a meeting with you last year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to our meeting, had you heard anything about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Only from the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A huge mass grave in your backyard and you never heard anything about it from any other source but the media; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: It was far from my eyes, far, far from my eyes. I wouldn't say it was close by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any discussion of the digging of those mass graves and how those bodies got there from anyone prior to our meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to Major Golic - excuse me - Major Nikolic about what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If bodies were being buried there, would that be a reference to the Serbian word "asanacija" if they were related to killed prisoners or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: The notion of asanacija is a broad concept. It could have been about that. Asanacija is carried out or implemented regardless of the status of the dead bodies. When you say "asanacija," it can apply to cattle, to animals as well, because asanacija is an action that is undertaken in order to prevent diseases from spreading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any information that in October of 1995, those hundreds and hundreds of bodies were dug up over a period of days and moved down south of the Srebrenica enclave, former enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever at a meeting where this was discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I was at meetings where this could have been discussed only superficially, but nothing specific at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A superficial discussion of moving hundreds and hundreds of dead bodies is a discussion of that subject, so if you could tell me when you heard a superficial discussion of that subject, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: At one of the meetings, mention was made, I don't know exactly when this was, I think October, that asanacija was being carried out, but no details were given when, how, why, under which circumstances, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now asanacija, is that something that is generally carried out in the middle of combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: It can be done in the middle of combat, and it can also be done after combat, depending on how long the combat goes on for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ever hear of anybody burying troops while they're being shot at by the enemy, burying bodies while they're being shot at in combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Not really. I haven't heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to exhibit number 712/A, and if you could take a moment to look at that. That's another group of minutes from the meeting, this time 16 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we don't want this to be on the public ELMO, but if we could have it on the ELMO, I'd appreciate it, as long as it's not going public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Witness. Now, you'll note that you were present by this record at this 16 October meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that at that meeting, there was a discussion, and I'll quote, "We are currently engaged in tasks issued by the army of Republika Srpska, General Staff, sanitation," in parentheses, the word in Serbian, "asanacija." Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Barely, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this comes under the heading of "Nikolic." That's the same Major Momir Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the chief of security for the brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: It should be the same one, yes. It should be him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I note here that this says that the task was issued by the General Staff or the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. Does that help you refresh your recollection as to this particular asanacija job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I really don't know how significant it was because I had absolutely nothing to do with that assignment; nor did I know what they were referring to, who was tasked to do that, using which means; nor did I provide any kind of assistance, so it was not my obligation to know what it was about. And I'm quite convinced that, at that meeting, no details were given, any details, and you can check by asking these other persons who are listed as being present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an officer in the army of Republika Srpska, is it not your duty when you are made aware of war crimes, to report those war crimes to your superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not your duty to close your ears at a meeting or ignore things that you don't want to hear; that's not the duty of a VRS soldier, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence objects to this question. My learned friend can rephrase it and ask him whether war crimes were discussed at meetings that the witness attended. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was merely responding to his response saying he didn't want to hear about it, but it's not an important issue. I think we can go on to others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now could we have Exhibit 161/4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: May I just comment on what Mr. McCloskey just said, because in a way he said that I didn't want to hear. I had nothing to hear there because I assert with responsibility that no details were given connected to that asanacija. And the concept of asanacija, as I have said, is nothing unlawful. It's an obligatory procedure that has to be engaged in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, perhaps we have to clear up this point now. What was the subject of discussion at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: As meetings were very brief, each person -- me, for instance, as battalion commander, would be given five minutes to report on the situation in my battalion. So that at those meetings, no details were entered into except if the commander had some queries about something important. If details had been discussed, then they probably would have been part of this document, would have been referred to in these minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember the expressions used, what was said in connection with asanacija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I just remember the term "asanacija" being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the circumstances, the places, the dates. Just the word was mentioned? Is that all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly. It says as it says here in the minutes. "We are now working under orders of the General Staff on asanacija," no further details. And I think that that was the method of work applied at such briefings. If somebody needed to brief the commander about details, he would have the time and place to do so after the meeting, to go to his office and discuss things with him in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So no one at that meeting, when the word "asanacija" was used, nobody asked for any clarifications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, everyone understood what was behind it, what it referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Not what was being concealed. We didn't know that anything was being concealed. We just knew that asanacija was being done. Now, what that term was implied, Major Nikolic should know, and if my commander had an interest, he probably asked him. But as I see here that the Main Staff ordered this, then I believe that even my commander need not have been informed, not to mention us lower-level officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, Mr. McCloskey, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would direct your attention to Exhibit 161/4 of a split aerial photo, and I'll direct your attention to the right side. This is dated 20 October, and this is in the area of the yellow dots from the previous map exhibit, and it shows an excavator digging on 20 October. The Prosecution has excavated that area and exhumed it and found many, many bodies. This is 20 October, four days after the meeting discussing asanacija. Does the term "asanacija" involve clearing the terrain of bodies like as depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I don't know what was implied, but in that period of time, my battalion and myself was focusing on the organisation of shift duty in the area of Trnovo so that I had absolutely no knowledge linked to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have any knowledge about prisoners taken by the VRS between the time period of July 12th and November 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Nothing specific. I didn't know anything in particular about those prisoners because I didn't have any. All I can talk about is the things that I eyewitnessed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We could also talk about what was discussed at this very same meeting, because if we go back to the exhibit of the meeting of October 13th, Mr. Nikolic also discusses that there are still remaining so-called Turks in the area and that they've taken statements from them and that, "We have seven." So were you listening to the discussion about prisoners taken between the time period I just asked about when Mr. Nikolic was discussing it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: There was no discussion about the prisoners, except that the fact was stated that they were being held as prisoners somewhere by our forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade was in fact getting prisoners all the way through the period of 12 July up until at least this period noted in this document, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I do not know about that. I didn't take any prisoners. Whether the others did or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go into closed session briefly, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's go into private session. Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 799, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the brigade had a military police unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the chief of that military police unit in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I think it was Dragisa Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I think he was a Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a colleague, colleague of yours that you communicated with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Not frequently. If I came across him, we would exchange greetings, jokes, but nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss with any members of the military police what they were involved in, in Pilica in July 16th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I have no idea where they were nor what they did nor was it my duty to know what the military police were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the military police from Bratunac transported prisoners to the Zvornik area brigade of responsibility and thereby assisted in the execution of prisoners in the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility, what commander would be responsible for those crimes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, why don't you ask who was the commander instead of saying which commander was responsible for these crimes because we're making judicial conclusions there. Perhaps you should just ask Who was the Commander of the police, or Who was responsible for the police, but not [In English] "What commander would be responsible for those crimes?" [Interpretation] I think that is passing judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can rephrase that, Your Honour, so it's not meant to pass judgement. What I was trying to get to is a hypothetical that would show us military responsibility and not any particular names of any individuals but just, in a situation where jurisdictions change, which jurisdiction becomes responsible for their soldiers in another jurisdiction that commit crimes, in this officer's opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then ask who was responsible for the soldiers, not for the crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you answer the question who was responsible for the soldiers in the situation that I've posed to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Specifically regarding the situation you have described to me, I don't know who could have been responsible. I assume that for activities carried out by subordinates, then the leader of that unit should be responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Judge Fouad Riad? No questions. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just a very few. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned at one point that you had an opportunity at some point to see parts of the column that was moving towards Tuzla. My question is simply: Did you know at that time -- it's referred to in several of the Bratunac Brigade command reports that there is this column attempting a breakthrough at particular points. Were you aware that the column consisted of -- basically two-thirds of it were civilians from Srebrenica or, in other words, not full-time soldiers but people who were fleeing from Srebrenica? I mean, was that well known in the area? Because it keeps being referred to as a breakthrough of the 28th. In fact, that was at the head, obviously, a third of it were members of the 28th Division, but two-thirds of it were people fleeing from Srebrenica, some armed lightly, some not armed at all. Was that well known?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: No, not at all. From our positions, we couldn't distinguish whether somebody was armed or whether someone was a civilian or not. And I can tell you that it was the practice in our brigade, and I assume also in the 28th Division, that all men were not in uniform because there was a shortage of uniforms. So there may be some confusion as to whether they were civilians or soldiers if you go by whether they wore uniforms or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So basically -- I know you had no combat contact with them, but basically in terms of knowing that they existed and were moving in a particular direction, they were regarded across the board as the 28th Division, right, as the enemy armed forces of the 28th Division; is that right? That's the way they were thought of in terms of the Brigade Command reports or whatever you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Now that so much time has gone by, my conclusion would be that the civilians who were safely evacuated from Potocari, they simply had no need to go with the column which it was assumed could encounter our forces and clash with them. So I would not assume that any civilians would move with that column, and especially not in such a high percentage as you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My other question is: With regard to the report of the minutes of -- I believe it was the October 16th meeting in which it's said that one of the parts of the brigade were carrying out assignments and asanacija with regard to orders from the Main Staff. My question is whether or not in your military experience it was usual or unusual for the Main Staff, rather than the battalion or the brigade, to be directing asanacija - however it's pronounced - of the particular battleground area in which a battalion or a brigade might have responsibility. Did the security part of the Main Staff generally take Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. over that function or was that a function that was more likely to be left to the local battalions and brigades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I am not aware of such cases of asanacija of the battleground, so I cannot tell you what the practice was. I really don't know whether it is customary, and I, generally speaking, don't know much about the concept of asanacija because I was trained in a different area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In this particular instance, however, although the main -- I gather from the report that although the Main Staff was giving direction to the operation, actually, soldiers from parts of the Bratunac Brigade were being used to do it, right? Otherwise, it wouldn't have been in the report. It was the soldiers from not your part but from other parts of the Bratunac Brigade that were doing the work in asanacija under the direction of the Main Staff. Is that the right interpretation of the report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I really don't know. As I have said, I cannot comment on that because I don't have any proper information. I don't know any details. I don't know who was doing it, following whose orders. I see from this record that it was the orders of the Main Staff, but who actually participated, how, using which devices, with what aim, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I do have a brief statement from the witness in his interview that would be directly relevant to Judge Wald's -- one of Judge Wald's questions, and so I would request leave of the Trial Chamber to just ask him about that one point. It would -- in that way we wouldn't have to bring him back on rebuttal or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is the Prosecutor referring to the statement made by the witness in Banja Luka in December last year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I am, and it's on the subject of the makeup of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has asked to obtain that statement. As we now have a witness testifying about his own statement, something will be shown to him from that statement, and I think that also would be in accordance with the ruling of the Chamber when other witnesses were testifying, the Defence would request to obtain that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has the Defence had an opportunity to examine that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We are in the situation we have been with other statements that witnesses have given to us that have testified. But this has to do with his statement of this witness to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, Mr. McCloskey is telling us that -- you know that the witness has information which can respond to a question put by Judge Wald to the witness; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I just clarify something?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Obviously I can't ask a question about a statement I've never seen, and apparently Mr. Petrusic can't ask a question about a statement he has never seen. You didn't cover this in your direct, so the most -- let me make an attempt just to ask, if I might, with the President's permission, just to ask the witness if he remembers saying anything previously in a previous statement about the makeup of the column, and then I think we should let it go at that, if that's satisfactory to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I didn't say anything in particular. I don't think that it differs in any sense from what I have just said. As far as I am concerned, he can refer to that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me address the parties. As you know, the principles that reign over the debate is fairness, and it is true that it is the truth that interests the Chamber. So the Chamber can call a witness, and there would be no sense in the Chamber, having learnt that there is something that may be important, should call the witness to come. What I think would be practical and would be fully in observance of the fairness of the proceedings is perhaps to say to the Prosecutor you can put your question, and the Defence has the possibility to respond, to cross-examine, in a sense, on that point, and the Judges may, too, so that we will resume the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. Perhaps we should begin with the Defence because it is a Defence witness that we have, but the Defence doesn't have the statement. So that would be my suggestion, to resume the discussion with the opportunity to cross-examine. I mean, fairness is of the utmost concern, and if we bear that in mind, we will be making a step towards establishing the truth. What would be your response, Mr. Petrusic, to my suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will be coming back again to the disputed issue. Putting aside the fact that the Prosecution has completed his examination-in-chief, that Your Honours have started the questions, so leaving that aside, we will again come up against the disputed issue, which is that the Prosecutor will show the witness a statement. The Defence has neither had that statement nor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting you. I am really sorry, but my suggestion would also mean that the Prosecutor puts the question. But without using the statement. So "I have heard" or "I have been informed," or something like that. He doesn't need to show the witness the statement. We forget that there is a statement; he just puts a question to the witness, and then the witness can be cross-examined on that particular question. Would you agree with what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, what do you think of that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can certainly give it a try. I understand I can base my question on what is in the -- in my possession but not read it, not quote it but paraphrase it in some manner to see the witness' response or just the very subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'll give the floor to Judge Wald. The question is that you cannot confront the witness with a statement. You cannot say, "You said this and now you're saying something else." You just accept the answer of the witness and then the Defence can cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sure you're familiar with it. I think, Mr. McCloskey, you say, "Did you, on a previous occasion, say, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah?" He may say no or give any explanation he wants and we have to let it go at that. And it doesn't get accepted into evidence, the statement, you're just asking him whether on a previous occasion he said something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand that, but I want to be careful. So I may say, "Did, on another occasion, did you say," and then say what I believe he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If it doesn't go on forever. I mean, if it's very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Very brief. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's very brief. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The parties agree that we proceed in this way: The Prosecutor puts a question to the witness and then the Defence can cross-examine the witness on the same point. In this way, the principle of fairness and adversarial system will be respected and there will be no prejudice to anyone. So, Mr. McCloskey, please proceed. Re-cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall in the questioning that we had several months ago Mr. Ruez was talking to you about the column, and you were talking to him about it, and do you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we come back to the same issue. The question in the way I understood your ruling and the suggestion of Judge Wald transcends that framework. It is not my intention to give him any suggestions or advice, on the contrary. Whatever was discussed with Mr. Ruez can be phrased in a separate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. McCloskey, I think that is my opinion. I speak in my own name, but my colleagues can also comment. You can put a question about the column. Go directly to the gist of the question and then we'll see what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall being asked about the column and the -- whether or not you took any action against the armed movement of the column, and your response -- do you recall this response: "As far as I was concerned, those are not troops. Those are lines of people. Columns which were moving on their way to the" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Petrusic on his feet. I'm sorry. When you're telling the witness "You remember that a question was put to you," are you referring to the question by Judge Wald or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. I was referring to Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Forget that. Forget that there was a statement. Put the question to the witness without reference to the statement. That is our ruling. That is our decision. The question has to do with the column. I know that. You have told us that it is about the column, following a question by Judge Wald. So regarding the column, put one, two, or three questions but without mentioning any previous statement that he may have made to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: There may be some confusion here. At least, it's my understanding, based on past experience here, that you can phrase a question along the following lines: "You testified in answer to Judge Wald that," whatever; you paraphrase what the witness just said. "Do you, on any previous occasion say that you considered the column to be mainly civilians," et cetera, something like that, and then just accept what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Visnjic. I'm told that the General needs a break. Is that what you want to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, but before that, if possible, I should like this question put by Mr. McCloskey that contains a direct quotation from a statement that we are not aware of should be redacted from the transcript as it has entered into the record. It is page 66 or, rather, 65, rows 24, 25; and page 66, rows 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we really need the break now for health reasons, so that we can think this over a little. But I'm told that the General needs a break. Are you confirming that, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we'll have a 10-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. May I very briefly explain my request? The main issue why we objected to Mr. McCloskey's question is the problem that we are having as we are unable to see whether the Prosecution, during this interview or interrogation or whatever we like to call it, whether his statement was faithfully recorded as we do not have the Serbian or the English versions. As we know, those statements are not interpreted simultaneously so that there are often very serious problems connected to translation. And that is one of the main reasons why we are objecting, because we have no way of checking whether what the witness told Mr. McCloskey was correctly translated, whether the Serbian and the English version of those statements coincide. That is one of the reasons, among others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we are turning round in a circle. You have mentioned the statement, so I don't know whether you are going to ask us to redact that reference. So I have to ask you something, Mr. McCloskey, to know exactly where we stand. My question is, what is the purpose of your question? Is it to complement an answer given by the witness in response to a question by Judge Wald on the column, that is, to give more information about that; or is it to impeach the witness because the witness answered you in one way and Judge Wald in another? So what is the purpose of your question? And maybe we should discuss this in the absence of the witness, but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The purpose, the basic purpose was for the Trial Chamber to be able to see what this witness would say in a response to what he said before in order that this matter regarding the column be fully flushed out. In my normal practice, I usually will first use something to refresh the person's recollection, and if it doesn't refresh their recollection and they have said something opposite to what is in this, then I would use it to impeach them. And in that regard -- however, in this particular situation, having it come after the Judge's questions, this is a new area for everyone. And I would -- I am content with what I believe Judge Wald was getting at, is that we just bring this up, see what he says about it, and then, and then stop and it's over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you think, do you think your purposes would be satisfied - mine would, I know - if you just more or less paraphrased the question along the line of, "Have you ever on a prior occasion said that you weren't going to" - I'm just using a - "pay attention to the column because it was full of civilians?" He'll say yes or no or give an explanation, and that will be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm fine with that. And of course, based on our previous practice, then we could show, even show the -- though we haven't used it directly, if counsel insists, we could show them the area so they could do the same thing. But that actually gets us into a whole other area, so maybe we should just avoid that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Why don't we end it with the question and let him answer it the way he wants to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Petrusic, because we're slightly in a different situation than on other occasions, we have here a witness called by the Defence, and the Prosecutor has the obligation to disclose statements of the witness to the Defence, but of the witnesses which the Prosecution is calling. Isn't that so? After all, that's a little different. In other words, the Prosecution does not have the obligation to disclose because this is a witness called by the Defence. So I think that we will manage to preserve fairness, which is our objective, and the adversarial principle by allowing the Prosecutor to put one or several questions on this issue. And since they haven't tendered the statement into evidence, the information that will be used is what the Prosecution obtains here in the courtroom, that is, the information -- that is the only information you need to cross-examine. There would be a problem if the statement were to be tendered into evidence because then it is evidence. But it is not going to be admitted as evidence. So I think under these conditions, the principles of fairness and adversarialism will be preserved. What do you think, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following what you have said regarding fairness and the adversarial principle, I agree with you, but if we resume the examination on the basis of the statement that was given, then the Defence has the right to say no on the basis of the Rules. If we are opening the debate on this issue to establish the credibility of the witness on the basis of that statement, that is, impeaching the witness, then the Defence is opposed and objects. So let me repeat. I agree if we're trying to establish the truth, that is, in accordance with your decision, the decision of the Chamber, and the suggestion of Judge Wald and yourself, that the witness be asked a concrete question regarding what he knows about the column or so on - let me not advise the Prosecution as to the wording - and then the Defence can, if it considers necessary, cross-examine the witness. I find that our situation is rather tricky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, we are really in an exceptional situation. I think that we're all trying to find a path which will contribute to the truth. It is not customary, after the questions of the Judges, to resume the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination of the same witness. So it is normal that we should have certain hesitations. So would you accept this suggestion of Mr. Petrusic or do you have another one? Otherwise, the Chamber will have to go back to its decision or change its decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't fully understand Mr. Petrusic's suggestion. I think I do understand Judge Wald's suggestion and I am perfectly prepared to say, "On a previous occasion," and then give a paraphrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Petrusic said that he agreed with the suggestion of Judge Wald. You also said that you agree with Judge Wald. So there must be a misunderstanding. Let me ask Madam Wald to formulate her suggestion, and then we will check because we do have a problem. Mr. Petrusic just said, "I agree with the proposal of Judge Wald." You also said that you agreed with Judge Wald, but, at the same time, you said you do not agree with Mr. Petrusic and he does not agree with you. So there must be some misunderstanding between the three of you. So Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My understanding of my suggestion was that Mr. McCloskey would say something along the following lines: "You just testified in response to Judge Wald's question that," paraphrase of what the witness just said right here in the courtroom. "Have you ever on a prior occasion said," a paraphrase. I would not -- given the context here, I would not get into the quotes; a short paraphrase, and then let the witness answer it as he wishes, over and out. That's my understanding of what I suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us try to come to an agreement. Mr. Petrusic, have you heard the suggestion? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let it be like that then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. McCloskey, do you agree with this proposal by Judge Wald which Mr. Petrusic agrees with it must be said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll certainly give it a try. I can't recall exactly all the details but I think I can give it a good try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You will find your own way within those frameworks, I hope. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in a question from Judge Wald regarding the column, you suggested in a manner that the column was not a civilian column. However, at a previous occasion did you tell someone that you did not think these were troops, that they were just people seeking safety or something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Can I try and resolve this dilemma by saying, Mr. McCloskey, I did not say that in that way. First of all, I should like you to bear in mind the fact that, from a large distance, I was able to observe that column with very poor quality optical instruments, that is, binoculars, and even then when I said what I said and now again I believe absolutely that it was a military column. Now, whether a certain percentage of civilians were among them, I don't know by what means I could have possibly noted that or made the distinction. You either misunderstood my previous statement or it was erroneously interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we're finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You managed; you found your way. So, Mr. Petrusic or Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, while we're still on the subject, I should like to remind you of my objection and request for the redaction of the quotation referred to by Mr. McCloskey and that has been recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in his answer, the witness mentioned it, so I don't think we can redact it. But in any event, we will not be using that statement as evidence, so there's no problem regarding the identity of the witness. And as we are not using it as evidence, we cannot use the statement of the Prosecutor, which cannot be admitted into evidence, anyway. So, Mr. Petrusic, do you have any cross-examination on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So no additional questions from Mr. McCloskey, so I think we have succeeded in our attempt to further the truth. Instead of having the witness come back again, I think we found a way out. I personally have a few questions, so it's my turn now. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said, you testified, that you had soldiers who were more or less 3 or 4 kilometres away from the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road. Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: Yes, at certain points in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because after all, your soldiers were not stationary; they were moving. I also think I understood you saying in an answer to Mr. McCloskey that there were transports of people coming from Potocari. Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DF
utterances.text: I assume there was, and I think that's what I said on the basis of what I learnt later on; otherwise, that road was a road with heavy traffic. So I couldn't note where the starting point was for a truck, for example, tractor, bus, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the following,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: about it; or did you learn from any other source, and if so, which source?

utterances.speaker: Did you learn about that movement because your soldiers told you
utterances.text: First of all, my soldiers informed me about -- from the observation posts that we had, that along the road there was dense traffic, but they could not have informed me as to the means, the equipment, or anything else that was being transported in those vehicles. And later on from the information media, as I said, or from the newspapers or television, I learnt that that was the road where the transport, among others, of the civilians and prisoners took place, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you learn about this from the media?

utterances.speaker: Did you learn about that movement because your soldiers told you
utterances.text: It was after the war and just before I started to follow this trial in the Slobodna Bosna newspaper or some media that reported on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this link between the traffic on the road and the transportation of people coming from Potocari, when did you link the two together?

utterances.speaker: Did you learn about that movement because your soldiers told you
utterances.text: Well, I might have linked it up in more detail only after I had insight into what the press was saying and the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When your soldiers informed you that there was a lot of traffic along that road - I think that is what I understood you to have said - did you understand also why there was that traffic and that movement?

utterances.speaker: Did you learn about that movement because your soldiers told you
utterances.text: I could only have assumed, but not in any detail because, as I say, it was not my duty to control the passage along that road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you could only make assumptions. What assumptions did you make at the time?

utterances.speaker: Did you learn about that movement because your soldiers told you
utterances.text: I assumed that it was exclusively civilians moving along that road which were being transported from the Potocari area further on, I did not know where. Because please believe me when I say, from that distance, whatever you have in the way of optical equipment, you wouldn't be able to distinguish what the person was being transported. That would be impossible. You couldn't distinguish that by looking through -- at it through binoculars. You could just distinguish whether it was a bus, truck, tractor, or something like that, but no other details at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were responsible for a military unit at the time. Did you know what the objective was of the military operation that you were involved in at the time?

utterances.speaker: Did you learn about that movement because your soldiers told you
utterances.text: I did not know the objective, and I said that in my previous statement, nor did I know at all about the attack on Srebrenica. It was only on the 6th of July that I learnt from the Chief of Staff who brought me the document and informed me about the situation in that territory. Up until then, it was my exclusive duty and obligation to put up a decisive, resolute defence in the area under my battalion's control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be said that you learnt that there was an operation on Srebrenica on the 6th when the Chief of Staff visited you?

utterances.speaker: Did you learn about that movement because your soldiers told you
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something else: Could you try to explain to us how come that there were trucks and buses and vehicles going past? Of course, as you said, you were not able to identify the persons inside, but in any event, there was a lot of traffic. Was it possible for the civilians themselves to be aware of that movement?

utterances.speaker: Did you learn about that movement because your soldiers told you
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you were a rather -- some distance away from the road, some soldiers 3 or 4 kilometres away. Let me put the question differently. Were there any civilians along the road, people living there, civilians who lived in the area?

utterances.speaker: Did you learn about that movement because your soldiers told you
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. I can only assume that there could have been some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, witness. You have just finished your testimony here. Thank you very much for coming, and we wish you a safe journey home. Thank you, Witness, for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher must pull down the blinds to lead the witness out because we have some other things to address. So don't move yet for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to address the question of documents that we have to deal with. I think that we have documents referring to this witness and the other documents of which we have a list. Perhaps it would be better to deal separately with the documents of Professor and General Radinovic, then the documents of this witness, and then we'll come back to the others. Would you agree with that, Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Visnjic, Mr. Cayley, and Mr. McCloskey? So Mr. Visnjic, for General Radinovic, I think that we have a list of your documents. Perhaps to facilitate things, we could give a number to this list and then refer to all the documents in that list under that number. Would you agree with that, Mr. Cayley --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- instead of going through the whole list?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have not actually seen this list, Mr. President, but I have been through all of the Defence exhibits for Professor Radinovic, and Mr. Visnjic and I have already agreed -- somebody is handing me a copy of the list now. I have been through all of these, and I have no objection to any of these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all that remains for me to do is to suggest that this list be numbered D161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you confirm that, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It will be Exhibit D161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic. I don't know whether this is a problem or not, but I have with me Defence Exhibit 160/A and B. No. I was going to say that it was not on the list, but it is, so I withdraw what I had just said. So the documents on the list -- Mr. Cayley, you have the list now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the documents figuring on the list which has been marked as D161 are admitted into evidence. So now, Mr. Cayley, do you have any observation to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The only observation I would make is something that's already been agreed between the parties, but just to put it on the record, that we agreed that there would be a deletion of a section, which I think has already been said. It was the section on law which Professor Radinovic addressed, and I think the Defence have agreed to submit a revised version of the report without that section. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Visnjic is nodding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic. I think it's paragraph 2, page something. It's slipped my mind. Is that correct? So we will have a new version of the same document which will be marked bis. Is that acceptable, Mr. Visnjic, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that we already have a number under bis, and it is the corrigendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the number could be 160/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar. Or ter perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I was just going to confirm that we did have D160 bis. Perhaps we could have D160 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Mr. Cayley, is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So have we regulated everything regarding the exhibits produced during the testimony of General Radinovic on the side of the Defence? Now, Mr. Cayley, do you have any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have four documents. They are Prosecutor's Exhibit 746, 759, 760, 762, and 777. I don't believe that Mr. Visnjic has any objections to those documents - we've already discussed the matter - and if that is the case, I would apply for those to be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a clarification, Mr. Cayley. I see on the transcript "746." Is it 746 or 756?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. It's 746.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the French interpretation, I think, made an error, but never mind, everything is clear now. So, Mr. Visnjic, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So these exhibits of the Prosecutor are admitted into evidence. Now, then, Mr. Petrusic, the testimony of this witness. Are there any exhibits to be tendered by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was Exhibit D25/1 that I wished to have admitted, and the other exhibits that the Defence used have been assigned numbers by the Prosecutor and those will be the numbers that they will go by. They were Exhibit -- OTP Exhibit 782, but after I hear from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but are you saying already that you have no objections or do you have objections? To speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objections at all with respect to the OTP exhibits in connection with this witness who was Witness DF.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey. And you have the advantage that you know in advance that there are no objections. So maybe you can take advantage of it and tender some more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I can just list the numbers of the new exhibits, though I should say they're already in evidence as part of Mr. Butler's very large collection. But since we referred to them specifically with these new numbers, we should have that in the record, and that is Exhibit 751, 782, 752, 778, 753, 799, 757, 758, 809, and 809 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you taken note, Madam Registrar, that there is no objection on the side of the Defence, and these exhibits are admitted into evidence. We now have this, an older set of documents, if I may call them that. You remember that we discussed previously some exhibits among which some required additional clarification. The question was addressed by Mr. Harmon and Mr. Petrusic, that is to say, Exhibit 792/A and "B." I think there was a memo from the translation service, and is it ready or not? Do you have any information about that, Mr. Harmon? The translation service, I think, should have provided a brief memo regarding a discussion we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you can bear with me for just a minute, Mr. President. I did receive a memo in respect of an exhibit. I don't have it at my disposal. There it is. I just don't have the exhibit number associated with this memo that is dated the 28th of November, 2000. Perhaps we could pass on this for just a moment and I can clarify this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Harmon. We also have another matter, and that is document 823. And the Defence said that it would comment on it the following week, and I think that week is already behind us, so I don't know if you remember. It regarded a revision of a translation of an order by the Drina Corps dated the 12th of May, 1995. And I think there was another exhibit, 823/A bis, which I think is a revised translation. In any event, the Defence said that it would prepare a definite answer. I don't know whether they have that answer now. Mr. Petrusic, have you any observations to make now about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it is a translation, just one moment, Mr. President, if I may, to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we cannot give an answer at this point. My colleague, Mr. Visnjic, has suggested to me, that is to say he said he probably asked the translation service. I know the document that it refers to, the May document, and the witness who commented on that document, but as far as I have been informed by Mr. Visnjic, the translation service has still not provided us with a revised translation, that is to say, no information about this translation. So we will have to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Petrusic, we will see what we can do. Let's go on now to Exhibit 830, 830, and Exhibit 838 bis, and I would like to ask the Prosecutor whether 838 bis should not be 830 bis? Regarding this exhibit, the Defence said the same thing, that it would pronounce itself the next week, and that was last week. So my question first to the Prosecutor. This document, 838 bis, is linked to document 830, and it seems to us that perhaps there was a typing error, that the number of the document should be 830 bis, but I would like to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My colleague who manages these affairs very capably for me informs me there is no 838. It is probably 830/A bis. Furthermore, that the translation service has completed their revision of this document, and that the Defence has been provided with a copy of the revision, but they needed time to review the revision. And that's where I left off, my office left off in terms of assessing the status of this particular document, so we're waiting for a reply from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we should address 830 bis and not 838, because in the transcript there is reference to 838 bis, so this needs to be corrected so that the document should bear the number 830 bis. Has the Defence got a position on this document? Because I think the document is dated the 11th of July, 1995, and there was a problem regarding the signature, the signature block, and which was revised, but the Defence said that it would take a position later. Is the Defence able to do so now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I owe the Trial Chamber an apology, and I hope you accept that apology, because I'm not in a position at this point to give my opinion. I haven't got the document at present, and I just did not have time to focus on that problem, which does not mean that in the coming period we shall not be informing the Trial Chamber as soon as possible of what we think. So we will be informing the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Surely. But after all, we cannot decide without having everything cleared up. If one party tells us that they will give us an answer, we need to have that answer to be able to decide. So I'm now going to review all the documents that are in this status before we make a decision. We have the Defence Exhibit 79, which is in the same position and is awaiting revision of the English translation. The same applies to Exhibit 81. Have we received revisions of the English translation? Do we have them down, Mr. Visnjic? Mr. Harmon has just told us that the translation service has completed all the revisions. I don't know whether Mr. Harmon was referring to revisions as well or just translations. Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Exhibit 79 is concerned, I think that it was a poor photocopy of that exhibit. We showed a better copy of this to the Prosecution, and as far as I was able to understand, they have no objections to it. By the time Mr. Harmon says whether he agrees with me, I can look up the next exhibit and give you my opinion there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know the answer in advance too, Mr. Visnjic, perhaps. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I maybe can assist the Chamber in this discussion of a large number of exhibits that were unregulated at the conclusion of the last trial session block. The Prosecution's office had objected to Defence Exhibits D27 through Defence Exhibit, as I recall, D74, and in that respect, we, the Defence and the Prosecutor's Office, have not had a meeting in the interim time to discuss attempting to regulate those exhibits. Mr. Visnjic did give me a clear copy of Defence Exhibit 97 to which I had previously objected because the name block had been removed from the bottom. So in respect of D97, I will withdraw my objection at this time, and I believe that a version of this exhibit should be entered into the record with the complete signature block or the typed block that was missing. So I think there should be, Your Honour, with the Defence's consent, a resubmission of the complete document and it should be given a bis number, and once that is done, I have no objection, as I say, to D97. Other than that, we have not gotten together to discuss attempting to regulate our differences on the other documents, and I think we would be in a position, since we have ended this week early, to quickly conclude those discussions this week, and when we resume on the next session, we would be able to inform the Chamber completely as to all of these outstanding exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that is a good suggestion because we are overstepping the time already by 15 minutes. So my suggestion would be the following: With the exception of this exhibit that Mr. Harmon has just mentioned, that is, Exhibit D97, if we add, "With the complete signature," that will become Exhibit D97 bis. If the Defence agrees, then we can go through a whole block of documents which have already been admitted into evidence. So my question is does the Defence agree with this suggestion that the document be called 97 bis once the whole signature block is added?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'm going to tell you which exhibits we can decide on straight away to clear things up a little. The exhibits which were, in a sense, admitted but which the Chamber did not declare admitted are Prosecution Exhibits 145/1, 367 bis, 765, 765/A, 765/B, 807, 812, 837. Defence exhibits which are also admitted, D74 and D76 through to D134. That's it. Also D135, D137/A and B, D138/B, D139/A [Realtime transcript read in error"D39/A"] and B, D140/A and B. I see on the transcript "D39." It's not D39, it's D139. So D139/A and B. So 541/A and B -- no, sorry. 141/A and B, 143/B, 144, 145, and 146. As you know, there was a question regarding Exhibit 836/1 through to 7. So 836/1 through to 836/7. These were documents related to General Krstic, and one could call them private documents. The position of the Chamber is that these documents were not relevant and, therefore, rules not to admit them into evidence. So those are the rulings of the Chamber for the moment. The documents that remain outstanding are Prosecution Exhibits 792/A and B; 830 and 830 bis, since we have clarified that 830 bis replaces the reference in the transcript to 838; also 823 and 823/A bis. The Defence exhibits that remain outstanding are D27 through to D71, as well as 79, 81, 109, 109, and for these three exhibits we have to see whether the revisions of English translations are ready or not. And finally, Defence Exhibit D132/A and B. So we have a set of documents that have already been admitted into evidence, and then there is this last set which are still outstanding and need to be discussed by the parties so as to clarify certain minor points. Mr. Visnjic, is there any response by the parties, or it is time to adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just see in line 24, Mr. President, that you said D142/A and B, but whereas in the transcript it says D132. Am I right that you said D142/A, B, that was the last number you read out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last number is 142, yes, 142. Which line is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty-four, page eighty-six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 24. Yes, you are quite right, thank you very much. It is 142/A and B, not 132/A and B. Mr. Harmon, any observations or remarks by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Not at this time, Mr. President. Should there be any, we will raise them at the next occasion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. I apologise, I hadn't intended to overstep our time limit. When we started this discussion, it was ten to three, and I hoped we would have finished quickly, so I apologise to the staff members, but we won't be seeing each other for the rest of the year, I think. So I think we will meet in January, so I take advantage of this opportunity to wish to those who do celebrate it, that is, Merry Christmas, though some celebrate it on the 25th of December, others on the 6th or 7th of January; and then also there is the new year, and all those who are able to celebrate it, I hope you have a festive celebration. So we will meet again next year; have a good holiday, and success in your work to all of you.
